title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
formal: Is Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every constants \(C>0\) and \(c\ge 1\), is there a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) whose shortest Extended Frege proof has bit length greater than \(C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\)? Here |\(\varphi |\) is the bit length of the explicitly written formula.
definitions:
Fix Boolean formulas over \(
eg\) and →, with → interpreted as material implication and variable indices encoded in binary. Use the Frege axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), together with modus ponens from A and \(A	o B\) to B. An Extended Frege proof of \(\varphi\) may additionally introduce an abbreviation variable e by the two extension axioms \(e	o 	heta\) and \(	heta 	o e\). Here e is fresh, absent from \(\varphi , 	heta\), and every preceding line; \(	heta\) uses original variables of \(\varphi\) and previously introduced extension variables. Extensions are thus acyclic definitions. Other proof lines are axiom instances or applications of modus ponens, and the last line must be \(\varphi\), with no extension variables. Lines may cite and reuse earlier lines arbitrarily: proofs are not required to be trees. Proof size is the full binary encoding length of all explicitly written formulas, extension definitions, and inference references; there is no depth or per-line-size restriction. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. This fixed presentation is polynomially equivalent to the usual Extended Frege systems, so changing a standard finite Frege basis does not change polynomial boundedness. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize propositional proof systems, polynomial simulation, and Extended Frege, proving robustness under the choice of standard rules and connectives.
Strong lower bounds emerge for weaker systems, while even unrestricted Frege lower bounds remain open. EF adds the ability to abbreviate and share formulas.

Pich and Santhanam establish conditional routes from EF proof lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The assumptions include formally provable computational statements; the result is not an unconditional EF lower bound.
Hsieh, Jain, Li, and Mathialagan obtain SNARGs for NP from derandomization, LWE, SXDH, and a bounded-arithmetic unprovability assumption concerning certificates of EF-hard tautologies.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations in extended polynomial calculus with a square-root rule. Its Section 1 explicitly distinguishes this from propositional Frege and EF lower bounds.

status_note: Explicitly open in the primary proof-complexity sources, including Alekseev’s June 2026 journal article. Research through 10 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution for unrestricted Extended Frege. The algebraic and conditional results cited here retain their stated scope.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\).

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

sentences: Extended Frege proves propositional tautologies while allowing reusable names for intermediate formulas.
The question asks whether some tautologies require proofs larger than every polynomial in their encoded statement length.
Reusable definitions can express shared computations compactly, defeating lower bounds based only on expanding formulas.
An unconditional result would be a major limitation on a powerful, efficiently checkable proof language.
The saved review emphasizes that proof size differs from proof-search time and that a lower bound for this particular system would not alone prove \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\).
